opus-5.5.text:
Well, it goes back to something I've been fascinated by since graduate school. People tend to assume that to get a robot to do something dexterous, you need perfect sensing: you have to know exactly where the object is, its exact shape, its exact pose, and then you plan a precise motion. But the real world is full of uncertainty. Sensors are noisy, objects aren't where you think they are, and friction is notoriously hard to model. So that approach is fragile.

A funnel is a beautiful counterexample. Think of pouring sand or coffee beans into a funnel. You don't need to know where any individual grain is. The geometry of the funnel takes a wide range of starting positions and collapses them into a narrow range of outcomes. It reduces uncertainty mechanically rather than computationally.

My PhD work was on orienting parts with a simple parallel-jaw gripper and no sensors at all. It turned out that for any polygonal part, there's a sequence of squeezes that will bring it into a unique final orientation, whatever orientation it started in. The physics of the squeezes does the work. That's a generalised funnel: an action, or a sequence of actions, that maps many possible states into one known state.

I think this matters a lot for dexterity because humans do it constantly without realising it. When you pick up a pen off a table, you don't compute its exact position. You sweep your fingers, you let it slide against your palm, you use the table as a constraint. Your hand exploits contact and compliance to funnel the object into a stable grasp. Factories have used this for a century, too, with vibratory bowl feeders, fixtures, chamfers on pegs so they slide into holes.

So for robotics, especially now, when there's so much excitement about learning from large datasets, I think funnels are an important complement. Learning can get you roughly to the right place, and well-designed funnels, whether in the gripper, the environment, or the motion strategy, can absorb the remaining error. That combination of approximate perception plus physical robustness is, in my view, much more likely to give us reliable dexterity than trying to model everything perfectly.

r001.rationale: The response says generalized funnels could improve robotic dexterity and reliability, and compares their use with human actions. It does not say they could bring robots toward human-level dexterity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the key insight is that dexterity doesn't have to come entirely from the robot. For decades, the dominant paradigm in robotics was: sense everything precisely, model everything precisely, and then execute a precise motion. And that turns out to be extraordinarily hard, because the real world is full of uncertainty. Your sensors are noisy, your models of friction and contact are wrong, your actuators have slop in them. If you're relying on precision at every step, errors compound and the whole thing falls apart.

A funnel is a way of getting around that. The classic example is the physical funnel in your kitchen: you don't need to aim a grain of rice precisely into a narrow opening. You just drop it somewhere in the wide mouth and the geometry does the rest. The shape of the funnel absorbs your uncertainty and converges everything to the same final state.

What I've argued for a long time, going back to work I did with Matt Mason and others in the late eighties and nineties, is that this idea generalises far beyond physical cones. If you push a part against a wall, the wall is a funnel. If you squeeze an object between two parallel jaws, the geometry of the object itself will rotate it into one of a small number of stable orientations, regardless of how it started. That's a funnel in the space of orientations. In fact, we were able to prove that for any polygonal part, you can design a sequence of squeezes using a simple parallel-jaw gripper that brings the part to a unique known orientation, with no sensors at all. The uncertainty just disappears because the mechanics are doing the computation for you.

I find that very beautiful, and I think it's deeply relevant now because we're in this moment where everyone is excited about end-to-end learning, collecting enormous datasets of demonstrations and hoping the policy will generalise. And some of that is working remarkably well. But robots still struggle with reliability. They might succeed eighty percent of the time, and for a lot of real applications that's not good enough. Funnels are one of the most powerful tools we have for closing that gap, because they give you robustness for free, from physics rather than from data.

So when I look at how humans are dexterous, I don't actually think it's because we have superb sensing and control. We're quite sloppy. What we do is exploit constraints constantly: we slide a key along the surface until it drops into the lock, we push a cup against the edge of the table to get our fingers under it, we use the environment to guide things into place. That's the hallmark of dexterity to me. And if we can get robots to discover and exploit these funnels, whether through analysis or through learning, I think that's where a lot of the real progress is going to come from.

r001.rationale: The response says that getting robots to discover and exploit generalized funnels is a source of real progress, and links funnels to how humans achieve dexterity.

astra-6.text:
Well, think about putting a peg into a hole. If you approach it as a pure positioning problem, you need to know exactly where the hole is and control the peg very precisely. But if the entrance is tapered, it guides the peg into place. A whole range of initial positions can lead to the same successful outcome. That’s the idea of a funnel: the physical interaction reduces uncertainty for you.

And it doesn’t have to be a literal funnel. You can push an object against a table or slide it into a corner. Those constraints help establish its position, even if your initial estimate was imperfect. Contact becomes something you use, rather than something you avoid.

That’s why I think this is such a useful way to think about dexterity. We don’t necessarily need ever more precise sensing and control at every instant. We can look for actions that succeed across a range of uncertainties, and let the geometry and mechanics do some of the work. The challenge is finding those actions and composing them into a sequence that accomplishes the task.

r001.rationale: The response explains how funnels can make robotic actions more robust to uncertainty and useful for dexterity, but it does not say that developing them could help robots approach human-level dexterity.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, think about putting a peg into a hole. If everything has to be aligned perfectly before you start, that’s a very demanding sensing and control problem. But if the entrance is tapered, you can be a little off, and contact with the sides guides the peg into place. The geometry does some of the work for you.

That’s the idea behind a funnel: a range of initial positions gets brought into a smaller range of final positions. And it doesn’t have to be a literal funnel. A robot can use a surface, a fixture, or contact with its own fingers to guide an object and reduce uncertainty about where it is.

I think that’s very important for dexterity because we often imagine it means controlling every motion with extraordinary precision. But part of being dexterous is choosing actions that make precision easier to achieve. Instead of fighting contact, you use it. The challenge is figuring out which combinations of geometry and motion will reliably guide the object where you want it to go.

r001.rationale: The response explains how funnels can aid robotic dexterity and says finding reliable geometry-and-motion combinations is a challenge, but it does not propose that developing generalized funnels could advance robots toward human-level dexterity.
